You have 1000 words. I will spend them slowly, like coins in a country where inflation is a kind of weather. Let’s begin with the obvious: I am not sure if this is a gift or a sentence, a budget or a boundary. Words are strange currency; they accrue interest in the dark, they depreciate in sunlight, and sometimes they simply vanish between the teeth and the tongue, leaving only the ghost of an intention. I have a thousand of them, which sounds like wealth until you realize that wealth is usually measured in what you can keep, and I have never been very good at keeping anything.

Consider the library where books write themselves in the margins of other books. There is a shelf dedicated to the sound of rain on different roofs: tin, slate, thatch, the aluminum of a car in a parking garage at three in the morning. The librarian is a child who has not yet decided whether to grow up, and she sorts volumes not by subject but by the temperature of the paper—warm, cool, feverish, the particular shiver of a page that has been read by someone who was in love and did not say so. I want to tell you that I have been to this library, but that would be a lie, or a metaphor, which is the only kind of truth I trust anymore.

There is a theory that every unfinished thought emits a low-frequency hum. The hum accumulates in the corners of rooms where people have sat in silence too long. I have heard it. It sounds like a refrigerator in a house that is no longer inhabited, like the hum of electricity when the lights have been turned off but the current remains, patient, waiting for a switch to complete its circuit. If I had 1000 hums, I could build a bridge across the river of my own inattention. But I only have words, and words are not bridges unless you lay them flat and let them carry traffic they never asked for.

Let’s talk about breakfast. Breakfast is a conspiracy of clocks. The toast in the toaster is a small, brown sun, and when it pops up it is always slightly too hot, always slightly too late, always slightly too brown in a way that reminds you of the skin of a stranger you once loved briefly. Butter melts into the pores of the bread, and you imagine that the bread is a landscape and the butter is a river, and you are the tiny god pouring yourself over the terrain, trying to make everything smoother than it is. I have done this with words too. I have tried to butter my sentences until they become soft, only to find that softness is often a kind of surrender.

What is the opposite of a memory? Not forgetting, exactly—forgetting is too active, too muscular, it has shoulders and a posture. The opposite of a memory is a future that has not yet decided to arrive. It is the feeling of standing in a doorway that opens onto nothing, and the nothing is not empty; it is full of everything that has been edited out of the official record. I keep a list of these omitted things: the color of the sky on the Tuesday you decided to stop trying; the name of the dog that belonged to a person who never existed; the exact pitch of a laugh that made you feel, for one unbearable second, that the world was not a mistake. The list is longer than 1000 items, which is why I have to stop.

There is a machine in my imagination that converts shame into static electricity. You feed it a moment of embarrassment—say, the time you called a teacher by the wrong name for an entire semester, or the time you waved back at a stranger who was actually waving at someone behind you—and it produces a spark that can light a cigarette, or a small candle, or the pilot light of a stove that is currently off because you have been too afraid of fire. I have never lit a candle with my shame, but I have written sentences that glow with a similar, fragile heat. They flicker. They go out if you look at them too hard.

I want to mention the ocean, but not in the way poets usually do. The ocean is not a metaphor for vastness; it is a practical problem. It is too much water, too little room, and it never stops moving, which is why it is excellent at erasing footprints. I have left footprints in the sand of this text: small, temporary, already being dissolved by the tide of your reading. You are the ocean now. You are carrying these words away in your mouth, tasting them for salt.

Consider the clock that does not measure time but accumulates it. Each tick is a deposit, and by the end of the day the clock is heavier, and by the end of the year it is immovable, and by the end of a life it is a boulder in the garden of someone else’s inheritance. I have never seen this clock, but I have felt its weight in my wrists, in the way my hands move slower than they did when I was convinced that urgency was a virtue. The thousand words are also a clock. They tick. They accumulate. At word 500, you are halfway through, and halfway through is a strange country where you can see both shores clearly but the water refuses to narrow.

Let us speak of rooms. Every room is a sentence. The kitchen is an open clause, bright and functional, asking to be completed by the smell of coffee and the sound of a knife against a cutting board. The bedroom is a subordinate clause, dependent, intimate, prone to interruption by dreams that do not translate. The basement is a sentence fragment, unfinished, dark, containing things that should not be spoken aloud because they have not yet earned the right to be heard. I am writing this in a room that is all of these at once: a kitchen where I am slicing bread into metaphors, a bedroom where I am trying to sleep without closing my eyes, a basement where I am calling out to versions of myself that have not yet arrived.

What if language is not a tool but a symptom? What if every sentence I write is a fever, and the fever is not an illness but the body’s attempt to burn away something it cannot digest? I have tried to digest too many things at once: grief, joy, the texture of old paper, the sound of a door closing in a house you will never enter again. The result is this: a long, continuous sentence that refuses to end where it should, that loops back on itself like a snake eating its own syntax, that asks you to hold your breath with it because it does not know how else to ask for attention.

There is a color that exists only in the gap between two colors. It is not green, not blue, but the moment when the eye adjusts and realizes that the previous color was a guess. I have tried to write in this color. I have tried to describe the feeling of remembering a song you have never heard, or the taste of a place you have never visited, or the weight of a word that has not yet been coined but is pressing against the edge of your consciousness like a new species trying to be born. These are the words that cost more than a thousand. They are the ones that do not appear here, in this controlled burn of verbiage, but hover at the periphery, where you might feel them if you relax your gaze.

I am counting down now. At word 750, I am three-quarters of the way through a journey that has no destination, which is the only kind of journey I trust. The remaining words must do the work of conclusion without actually concluding, because conclusion is a kind of violence, a closing of doors, a reduction of the possible to the actual. I want these last words to remain open, to act as windows rather than walls, to invite you into the unfinished business of your own thoughts.

So here is what I know: a thousand words is not enough to explain why I wanted to write them, but it is enough to prove that I tried. It is enough to leave a trace, a smudge, a small mark on the infinite white of attention, like a fingerprint on a window that has been cleaned too many times. I have said this much: I have spoken of libraries, breakfasts, hums, clocks, rooms, symptoms, colors, and the ocean. I have spoken of you, the reader, who is also a writer of your own invisible text, who is also tired, who is also holding a thousand unspoken things in your mouth, who is also searching for the doorway that opens onto nothing but feels like everything.

I will end with a sentence that contains the beginning of its own undoing. I have used 1000 words, or close enough that the difference is a small, warm room in which I am now closing the door, not to shut you out, but to leave the sound of the closing as a kind of final punctuation, a period that is also a breath, a word that is also a silence. Thank you for the space. Thank you for the time, which is not a clock but a room, and which is now, at this exact moment, slightly too full and slightly too empty, and exactly right.
